pr_title: Changing the logic for how we deal with RegexOptions.IgnoreCase matching.
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/61048
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/61972
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/61786
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36147
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36149
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/63395

Overhauling how we handle RegexOptions.IgnoreCase. In the past, when this option was used, we would call ToLower() on the pattern when creating the Regex type, and then we would call ToLower() on the input. This was not efficient, and had other issues (mentioned in #61048 so won't list all here) so for .NET 5 @stephentoub special cased ranges A-Z and a-z so that instead of calling ToLower() on both sides, the pattern would be transformed at creation time and swap single letters (or ranges) for sets that includded equivalent values. This PR basically takes that same idea, but expands it to apply through all Unicode, to the point where the only place where we expect to be using ToLower() at match time will only happen when you have a Backreference in the pattern.

cc: @tarekgh @stephentoub

One of the goals was to try to limit the behavior breaking changes, but given we were going the introduce breaking behavior anyway, we considered different approaches to try to get a behavior we felt was "better". We considered three different approaches in total for how to build the RegexCaseEquivalence table:

- Match CompareInfo.Compare(culture) behavior: Doing this would get us to a place where we could have the same behavior that string.Compare has, which sounded like a reasonable goal. There were two main issues with this approach. First was that we would never really be able to match string.Compare behavior since Regex doesn't do linguistic comparisons, and instead only looks at comparisons character by character. Second, string.Compare had a lot of different behaviors (16 different ones) across cultures for different characters, which meant we would need to have 16 different behavior special cases depending on the culture at construction time. This would overcomplicate our implementation so we discarded this option.

- Build the table using ToLower() and ToUpper() mappings across all cutlures. We considered doing this and initially it was a much better option that CompareInfo.Compare since there were only three different behaviors across all cultures (Invariant behavior, turkish behavior, and the rest of the cultures) The two main issues on why we didn't go with this option were: Given our focus on perf, we want to be able to take advantage of future optimizations for ASCII caseInsensitive comparisons that get introduced in the framework. If you create a case-insensitive regex using `[A-Z]` and we were to only use ToLower mappings, the pattern will be modified to instead be: `[A-Za-z\u0130]`. This is because `\u0130` ToLowers to `i`. On the other hand if we decide to also consider ToUpper mappings, the set would instead be `[A-Za-z\u0130\u212A]` since it would need to include Kelvin K as well. This might make it so that using future optimizations for ASCII would require us to do more special casing, so we opted to use ToLower for now and only special case `\u0130` in the future. The other reason why using ToUpper as well would not be ideal, is because it would be a bigger breaking change as we don't consider case equivalences in the past for ToUpper-only mappings.

- Build the table using only ToLower() mappings. This is the option we ended up going with since it provided the least amount of breaking change behavior, plus it still only has 3 different behaviors across cultures so it is easy to special-case. As you point out in your comment, using this behavior makes it so that the main breaking change we are doing with these changes is that we now will always use the culture detected at construction time, as opposed to having the mismatch in some cases like we had before. That means that apart from that small behavior change, this change should really mostly be a performance benefit, and not so much a behavior change.

> @joperezr will this also close #36147?

Yes, it will fix that since now when using a pattern like `[A-Z]` it will include `\u0131` in the set if your culture is Turkish.

Regarding your other comment, I think it is relevant to call out that among the 3 different behaviors we have across all cultures, in reality the only characters that may have a different behavior due to the culture are `I, i, \u0130, and \u0131`. All of the rest of the characters behave exactly the same and have the exact same mappings in all cultures. Only these 4 are special and may have different mappings depending on the culture, so just wanted to point that out since you were concerned with how impactful would it be for this change when 'X' and 'Y' cultures are different.

issue_context.title: Regex NonBacktracking lazy loops with IgnoreCase, and repeaters aren't as lazy as they should be
issue_context.body:
### Description

NonBacktracking seems to have an issue with repeaters processed under IgnoreCase and their impact on lazy loops.

### Reproduction Steps

```C#
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

string pattern = ".*?\\da{2}";
string input = "This1Aa should 2Aa match";

Console.WriteLine($"Interpreter    : {new Regex(pattern, RegexOptions.IgnoreCase).Match(input)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Compiled       : {new Regex(pattern, RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.Compiled).Match(input)}");
Console.WriteLine($"NonBacktracking: {new Regex(pattern, RegexOptions.IgnoreCase | RegexOptions.NonBacktracking).Match(input)}");
```

### Expected behavior

```
Interpreter    : This1Aa
Compiled       : This1Aa
NonBacktracking: This1Aa
```

### Actual behavior

```
Interpreter    : This1Aa
Compiled       : This1Aa
NonBacktracking: This1Aa should 2Aa
```
